object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account in the system, identified by a unique sequential six-digit account number. Each account represents either the initial relationship with a company or a new relationship if the company returns after closure.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off... Six digits, sequential, never reused.
Unpack "customer" first. What is a customer in the system? An account.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: A six-digit sequential identifier for an Account, never reused even if an account closes and reopens.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number... Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement between an Account and the company that specifies what Account pays on what billing cycle for what Product. Each subscription has a current price plan (which may change over time via plan changes), a start date, optional end date, billing period, and status.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Subscription ID. The account. The product. The price plan. Start date. End date, sometimes. Billing period. Status... Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a Subscription, generated and prefixed with 'SUB'.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offered by the company. Currently three products exist: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT. An account can have at most one active subscription per product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.
We now sell three, and an account can have a subscription to each of them at once.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: A code identifying a Product. Valid codes are CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: A billing artefact that specifies the price a customer pays and how often (monthly or annual). Each price plan entitles exactly one feature bundle. Multiple price plans can point to the same bundle (e.g., monthly and annual variants, legacy versions, or bespoke enterprise pricing).

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
Every price plan gives you exactly one feature bundle... And there are price plans that exist only for one customer. Bespoke enterprise pricing. Those still point at a bundle.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: A code identifying a PricePlan. Examples include CORE-MO-49 and CORE-AN-490.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code... CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature bundle that specifies what a customer gets: the number of seats, whether they get API access, whether they get SSO, etc. Identified by name. Multiple price plans can point to the same bundle, and a bundle can exist before any price plans are created for it.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: The unique name of a FeatureBundle. Valid names are Starter, Professional, and Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to the price plan on a subscription. Each change records the effective date (which may differ from the date the change was requested), the new price plan, and who requested it. A subscription starts with no plan changes, and accumulates them over its life.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates... It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a PlanChange.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a Subscription. Exactly one status applies to every subscription at all times.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency at which a Subscription is billed. Either monthly or annual, never both on the same subscription, never neither.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual... Only those two... Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a Subscription begins. This is mandatory and must be present when a subscription is created.

source_references.excerpt: Start date... Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a Subscription ends. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date and run until cancelled. Fixed-term subscriptions (usually enterprise deals) have an end date agreed up front. Can be set by cancellation to indicate when paid access runs through.

source_references.excerpt: End date, sometimes... An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date a PlanChange takes effect. This may differ from the date the change was requested.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person or role who requested a PlanChange. Recorded on the change record.

ambiguities.description: Multiple concepts called 'plan': The transcript identifies at least three distinct meanings of the term 'plan': (1) price plan (billing artefact specifying price and frequency), (2) feature bundle (what customer gets, shown on pricing page), and (3) sales deal (what the sales team negotiates). The model captures the first two as separate entity types but does not attempt to model the third (sales deal). It remains unclear whether there are additional plan-like concepts in the system.

source_references.excerpt: Now, plan. You both used the word... When I say plan I mean what the customer gets... And I mean the billing artefact... the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated
Only that we still call three different things 'plan' and this document won't fix that... It won't. But it'll at least name them separately

ambiguities.description: Account reuse and identity over time: When an account closes and the same company returns, they receive a new account number and are treated as a new customer for reporting. However, it is unclear whether the business intends to model this as a genuine identity loss (the returning company is a different entity) or whether a supertype relationship should track 'the same company across multiple account lifespans.' The choice affects whether to model a Company or Organization entity and how to handle historical continuity.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting... It drives finance the other way. If we reused numbers, revenue recognition would be a nightmare.
Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: Subscription paused state: Priya states that paused is 'a flag' (boolean), not a status, yet it behaves like a status and causes bugs in filtering (queries for 'active' subscriptions incorrectly include paused ones). It is unclear whether paused should be modeled as: (a) a boolean attribute separate from status, (b) a fifth status value, or (c) a separate fact type (e.g., 'Subscription is paused'). The model records the four stated statuses but does not capture the paused flag.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term annual subscription cancellation policy: The system behavior is clear (cancellation sets end date to paid-through date and access continues), but the business rule is undecided. Tom reports that four customers received refunds in the last quarter after escalation, implying a de facto policy. Sam notes this affects revenue recognition (whether to record as contra-revenue or refund liability). Priya states this must be decided by finance and legal, not captured here. The model records system behavior but explicitly does NOT model a refund concept, leaving the business rule undefined.

source_references.excerpt: Mid-term cancellation on annual plans... The system rule is clear, and what's unclear is whether the system rule is the business rule... That's exactly it... Then I'm parking it explicitly. What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Plan change request date vs. effective date: The model captures that a plan change has both an effective date (when it takes effect) and an implicit request date (when it was made). The transcript states 'someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month,' but does not explicitly name or require a request date field. It is unclear whether request date should be modeled as a separate fact type or attribute on PlanChange.

source_references.excerpt: because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates. Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

ambiguities.description: MRR derivation and reporting layer: Sam states MRR is 'on the subscription in the reporting layer' and is 'worked out' from price plan and billing period, not stored in the source system. The facilitator explicitly decides not to model MRR as a stored attribute. However, it remains unclear how the reporting layer is structured and whether any derived values should be explicitly modeled in the conceptual model, or if all derivations should be omitted.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR... Is MRR stored on the subscription? It's on the subscription in the reporting layer... It's worked out... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts

ambiguities.description: Subscription start date and billing cycle timing: The model captures that every subscription has a start date (mandatory) and a billing period (monthly or annual). However, it is not explicitly stated whether the start date is the date the subscription becomes active, the date the first billing cycle begins, or the date the customer signs up. If billing cycles are staggered relative to the start date (e.g., start Jan 15, first invoice due Feb 1), this would affect revenue recognition and may require additional modeling.

source_references.excerpt: Start date... Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

ambiguities.description: Feature bundle scope and evolvability: The model identifies three current bundles (Starter, Professional, Enterprise) but does not capture whether bundles are versioned over time. If feature content changes (e.g., seats, API availability, SSO), does a customer's existing subscription stay on 'the old Professional' or move to 'the new Professional'? This affects whether bundle should have a temporal dimension or version identifier.

source_references.excerpt: Yes -- we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy.

ambiguities.description: Unique identification of price plans: Price plans are identified by plan code, but it is not stated whether plan codes are globally unique across products or scoped by product. For example, could CORE-MO-49 and ANALYTICS-MO-49 both exist? The transcript gives CORE-MO-49 and CORE-AN-490 as examples but does not clarify the scope of uniqueness.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code... CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

ambiguities.description: Contact vs. Account relationship: Priya states 'Email is on the contact, not the account.' This implies a Contact entity exists (with email), but the model does not capture Contact or its relationship to Account. It remains unclear whether Contact should be modeled, whether one Account can have multiple Contacts, whether Contact identification scheme, and how Contact relates to the subscription agreement.

source_references.excerpt: Email is on the contact, not the account.

ambiguities.description: Constraint storage: The facilitator notes that the constraint 'one active subscription per account per product' was 'enforced at the database level' after the Halloway incident. It is unclear whether this constraint is enforced at the application logic layer as well, what happens if the constraint is violated (error message, rejection, silent failure), and whether the model should distinguish between constraints enforced at the database, application, or both levels.

source_references.excerpt: And that's when the constraint went in... One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.
